\chapter{Here, There, and Where}
\label{ch:ur-here-there-and-where}
\hlchaptermodality{24}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can put a demonstrative in front of a postposition, and I can say where something is and where it is not.}

\ur{کہاں} has been askable since chapter seventeen and unanswerable ever since. \ur{یہاں} and \ur{وہاں} answer it, and \ur{اس} and \ur{ان} let the demonstratives the book already owned stand in front of a postposition for the first time.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[is]{\ur{اس} (is) — this, before a postposition}

\label{lesson:UR-C24-is}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{this} and \textbf{that}. Then say what happens to \textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} when a postposition follows it.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the word that heads a reason — \emph{kyūṅki}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{اس}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{یہ} \ur{کمرہ}} — \emph{yih kamrā} — this room.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{اس} \ur{کمرے} \ur{میں}} — \emph{is kamre meṅ} — \textbf{in this room.}
\end{quote}

The demonstrative does what the noun does. \textbf{\ur{یہ}} is the direct shape; \textbf{\ur{اس}} is the oblique one, and it appears for the same reason \textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} became \textbf{\ur{کمرے}} — a postposition is coming.

So the whole phrase shifts together. Pointer, adjective and noun all move into the oblique, and only then does the postposition arrive:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{اس} \ur{کالے} \ur{کمرے} \ur{میں}} — \emph{is kāle kamre meṅ} — \textbf{in this black room.}
\end{quote}

Three words changed shape for one little word standing after them. That is what Urdu does instead of case endings.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the far one too}]
\textbf{\ur{وہ}} has the same pair, and its oblique is \textbf{\ur{اس}} as well in the singular — Urdu's near and far demonstratives collapse into one oblique form and are told apart by context:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{meaning} & \textbf{direct} & \textbf{oblique} \\
\midrule
this & \textbf{\ur{یہ}} & \textbf{\ur{اس}} \\
that & \textbf{\ur{وہ}} & \textbf{\ur{اس}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Which means \textbf{\ur{اس} \ur{کو}} and \textbf{\ur{اس} \ur{پر}} are available for both, and a learner who has been unable to say \emph{to him} since chapter one can now say it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair — \emph{yih kamrā}, then \emph{is kamre meṅ}
  \item the whole phrase moving together — \emph{is kāle kamre meṅ}
  \item on its own — \emph{is ko}, \emph{is par}
  \item \emph{is kām ke liye} — for this work
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the oblique of \textbf{\ur{یہ}}? (\textbf{\ur{اس}}.) And of \textbf{\ur{وہ}}? (\textbf{\ur{اس}} as well.) What else in the phrase changes shape with it? (\textbf{The adjective and the noun} — everything before the postposition.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[un]{\ur{ان} (un) — those, and him respectfully}

\label{lesson:UR-C24-un}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{in this room}. Then name the three words for \textbf{you} and say which one is the respectful one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{ان}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ان} \ur{کو}} — \emph{un ko} — \textbf{to them.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ان} \ur{کمروں} \ur{میں}} — \emph{un kamroṅ meṅ} — \textbf{in those rooms.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{اس}} is the oblique for one thing. \textbf{\ur{ان}} is the oblique for more than one, and it serves both \textbf{\ur{یہ}} and \textbf{\ur{وہ}} exactly as \textbf{\ur{اس}} does.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a plural that is not about number}]
Here is the part a learner has to be told, because guessing it wrong is rude.

Chapter three taught that Urdu says \textbf{\ur{آپ}} to somebody it respects — a plural form used for one person. It does the same thing about somebody:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ان} \ur{کو}} — \emph{un ko} — \textbf{to him} or \textbf{to her}, respectfully.
\end{quote}

So \textbf{\ur{ان} \ur{کو}} is \emph{to them}, and it is also \emph{to him}, and which one it is depends entirely on who you are talking about. Said of a mother, a teacher, an elder, \textbf{\ur{ان}} is the only correct choice, and \textbf{\ur{اس}} would be heard the way calling a stranger by their first name is heard.

The safe habit while you are learning: \textbf{\ur{ان}} for anybody older than you, \textbf{\ur{اس}} for children and for things.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{un ko}
  \item the two obliques side by side — \emph{is ko}, \emph{un ko}
  \item of a mother, respectfully — \emph{māṅ … un ko}
  \item \emph{un kamroṅ meṅ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the plural oblique? (\textbf{\ur{ان}}.) Does it always mean more than one person? (\textbf{No} — it is also the respectful \emph{him} or \emph{her}.) And which word for \textbf{you} works the same way? (\textbf{\ur{آپ}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yahāṅ]{\ur{یہاں} (yahāṅ) — here}

\label{lesson:UR-C24-yahan}



\begin{quote}
Ask \textbf{where?} Then say \textbf{this}, and look at how the two words begin.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{یہاں}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میں} \ur{یہاں} \ur{ہوں}} — \emph{maiṅ yahāṅ hūṅ} — \textbf{I am here.}
\end{quote}

Chapter seventeen taught \textbf{\ur{کہاں}} — \emph{where?} — and this book has had no way to answer it ever since. A learner could ask the question and could not receive the reply.

Look at the two words together. \textbf{\ur{کہاں}} and \textbf{\ur{یہاں}} share their ending, and differ only in the head: \textbf{\ur{ک}-} asks, \textbf{\ur{یہ}-} points near. That is not a coincidence to be memorised — it is a frame.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the frame, two thirds filled}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{head} & \textbf{frame} & \textbf{word} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ur{ک}-} asking & thing & \textbf{\ur{کیا}} \\
\textbf{\ur{ک}-} asking & place & \textbf{\ur{کہاں}} \\
\textbf{\ur{یہ}-} near & thing & \textbf{\ur{یہ}} \\
\textbf{\ur{یہ}-} near & place & \textbf{\ur{یہاں}} \\
\textbf{\ur{وہ}-} far & thing & \textbf{\ur{وہ}} \\
\textbf{\ur{وہ}-} far & place & \emph{next lesson} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Chapter seventeen already showed you that \textbf{\ur{کیا}}, \textbf{\ur{کون}} and \textbf{\ur{کہاں}} are one family. This is the other half of that observation: the \emph{answers} are a family too, built on the pointing heads, and the ending is shared across both.

One cell is still empty, and you can already guess what goes in it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maiṅ yahāṅ hūṅ}
  \item the question and its answer — \emph{kahāṅ?} … \emph{yahāṅ}
  \item with a room in it — \emph{kamrā yahāṅ hai}
  \item the two endings, side by side — \emph{kahāṅ}, \emph{yahāṅ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do \textbf{\ur{کہاں}} and \textbf{\ur{یہاں}} share? (\textbf{Their ending}.) What is different? (\textbf{The head} — asking against near.) And which cell of the frame is still empty? (\textbf{The far one}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vahāṅ]{\ur{وہاں} (vahāṅ) — there}

\label{lesson:UR-C24-vahan}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{here}. Then say \textbf{that}. Now guess this lesson's word before you read on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{وہاں}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{وہ} \ur{وہاں} \ur{ہے}} — \emph{voh vahāṅ hai} — \textbf{he is there.}
\end{quote}

If you guessed it, that is the lesson. The frame is closed:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{head} & \textbf{thing} & \textbf{place} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ur{ک}-} asking & \textbf{\ur{کیا}} & \textbf{\ur{کہاں}} \\
\textbf{\ur{یہ}-} near & \textbf{\ur{یہ}} & \textbf{\ur{یہاں}} \\
\textbf{\ur{وہ}-} far & \textbf{\ur{وہ}} & \textbf{\ur{وہاں}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Six words, three heads, two frames — and every one of them was predictable from the shape of the others.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what a place word can now do}]
These two words and the postpositions of the last chapter answer the same question at different resolutions:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ur{وہاں}} — \emph{there}, gesturing
  \item \textbf{\ur{اس} \ur{کمرے} \ur{میں}} — \emph{in that room}, naming
\end{itemize}

And the denial you already own works on both, because \textbf{\ur{نہیں}} goes in front of the verb wherever the verb is:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{وہ} \ur{وہاں} \ur{نہیں} \ur{ہے}} — \emph{voh vahāṅ nahīṅ hai} — \textbf{he is not there.}
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{voh vahāṅ hai}
  \item the pair — \emph{maiṅ yahāṅ hūṅ}, \emph{voh vahāṅ hai}
  \item the denial — \emph{voh vahāṅ nahīṅ hai}
  \item gesturing and naming — \emph{vahāṅ}, then \emph{is kamre meṅ}
  \item the whole frame — \emph{kyā, kahāṅ; yih, yahāṅ; voh, vahāṅ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the three heads? (\textbf{\ur{ک}-} asking, \textbf{\ur{یہ}-} near, \textbf{\ur{وہ}-} far.) What ending do the place words share? (\textbf{-\ur{اں}}.) And where does \textbf{\ur{نہیں}} go in \emph{he is not there}? (\textbf{In front of the verb}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[is · un · yahāṅ · vahāṅ]{Here, there, and where}

\label{lesson:UR-R24-here-there-where}



\begin{quote}
Two demonstratives learned a second shape in this chapter and two place words closed a frame. Name all four, and say which of the four is also a mark of respect.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the obliques — \emph{is ko}, \emph{un ko}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kahāṅ?} … \emph{yahāṅ} … \emph{vahāṅ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} gesturing, then naming — \emph{vahāṅ}, then \emph{us kamre meṅ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the word that asks \emph{why} — \emph{kyūṅ}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — everything the book owns, pointed at and placed}
Two chapters ago nothing in this book could be anywhere and no demonstrative could stand in front of a postposition. Run the distance, cold.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the question family — \emph{kyā}, \emph{kaun}, \emph{kahāṅ}
  \item the answer family — \emph{yih}, \emph{yahāṅ}; \emph{voh}, \emph{vahāṅ}
  \item the drinks, placed — \emph{chāy yahāṅ hai}, \emph{pānī vahāṅ hai}
  \item the whole phrase bending together — \emph{is kāle kamre meṅ}
  \item people, respectfully and not — \emph{is ko}, then of a mother, \emph{un ko}
  \item the family, placed — \emph{māṅ yahāṅ haiṅ}, \emph{bahan vahāṅ hai}
  \item the weather — \emph{sardī hai}, and \emph{yahāṅ sardī hai}
  \item a denial — \emph{voh yahāṅ nahīṅ hai}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the oblique of \textbf{\ur{یہ}} and of \textbf{\ur{وہ}}? (\textbf{\ur{اس}} for both.) What is the plural oblique? (\textbf{\ur{ان}}.) When must you use \textbf{\ur{ان}} about one person? (\textbf{When you respect them}.) And what do \textbf{\ur{کہاں}}, \textbf{\ur{یہاں}} and \textbf{\ur{وہاں}} share? (\textbf{Their ending}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
